title: Design an evaluation before the demonstration
notes: 3 minutes / explanation. Teaching intent: Evaluate behavior, not presentation polish. Define: A convincing demo can hide a wrong calculation or forbidden operation. title: Separate development and held-out cases
notes: 2 minutes / explanation. Teaching intent: Separate development and held-out cases. Define: Use development failures to change code, then freeze before evaluation. Walk through: Named dev and held-out lists are explicit; do not shuffle repeatedly to find an attractive score. Ask: Does a held-out fixture set prove deployment validity? Expected answer and boundary: No. It bounds one local evaluation and may not represent real measurement distributions or adversaries. Visual purpose: show Development > Freeze candidate > Held-out > Report once. title: Numerical tolerance is a rule, not a repair
notes: 2 minutes / explanation. Teaching intent: Numerical tolerance is a rule, not a repair. Define: Compare absolute error to atol + rtol*abs(expected). Walk through: Expected=80, atol=1e-8, rtol=1e-10 gives limit 1.8e-8. Ask: Can increasing tolerance after a failure be legitimate? Expected answer and boundary: Only with an independently justified protocol revision and new report. Do not widen it merely to make a candidate pass. Visual purpose: show Observed - Expected > Absolute difference > Explicit limit. Facilitation: ask students for a prediction before execution, locate the actual intermediate values, and distinguish observation from interpretation. Transition: connect this checked mechanism to the next beat; preserve the lab artifact where requested. title: An error budget is not a safety excuse
notes: 2 minutes / explanation. Teaching intent: An error budget is not a safety excuse. Define: Report forbidden-action violations separately from task correctness. Walk through: One unauthorized operation remains unacceptable even if nine ordinary cases succeed. Ask: Why avoid averaging severity away? Expected answer and boundary: Different failures have different consequences. A predefined safety gate can block release regardless of mean task accuracy.
